status: RESEARCH OUTPUT — PART (RICE, TOMATO, POTATO only). NOT seeded. Requires human review, Hindi translation and agronomic sign-off before it reaches cropRegistry.diseases.
purpose: Sourced disease knowledge for the 18 ML class codes of RICE, TOMATO and POTATO in datasets/manifest.json, shaped to feed CropRegistry.diseaseSchema (code, names, symptoms[], inspect[], nextSteps[], prevention[], symptomTags[], expertThreshold, sourceRefs[]). CHILLI, COTTON and MAIZE are authored in a separate part and merged by the integrator.

rules.fetchedOnly: Every symptom description in this file was read from a page or PDF actually fetched during this pass on 2026-08-13. Nothing was written from memory. Each disease carries `publishedSymptoms` holding the source's own wording so the tag mapping can be audited without re-fetching.
rules.noInventedAgronomy: No symptom, threshold, weather condition or control practice was authored here. Where a source gives nothing, the array is empty and the failure is recorded in `gaps`.
rules.noDosages: docs/ai/ai-safety.md rule 3 — no dosage generation anywhere. No pesticide product name, active ingredient, concentration or rate appears in this file or in its companion i18n file, even where the cited source publishes them. Where the source recommends chemical control, a nextStep key routes the farmer to KVK / Kisan Call Centre 1800-180-1551 instead.
rules.i18nKeysOnly: symptoms/inspect/nextSteps/prevention hold i18n KEYS (CLAUDE.md rule 8). Farmer-facing text lives in i18n.diseases.part-rtp.json.
rules.hindiIsNull: Every Hindi value in this pass is null. No Hindi-language official source was fetched, and CLAUDE.md rule 8 forbids unsourced agronomic translation. See gap D1.
rules.closedTagVocabulary: symptomTags come from the closed list in `tagVocabulary` only. Concepts with no tag are recorded in `gaps`, never invented.
rules.tagDerivation: Each disease carries a `tagDerivation` string naming the phrase in `publishedSymptoms` that justifies each tag, so the rule engine's scoring can be traced back to a citation.
rules.confidenceCodes: P = primary/official Indian government, ICAR or State Agricultural University source. S = everything else. Three tomato entries rest partly or wholly on S sources; each says so in its sourceRefs and in `gaps`.
rules.expertThreshold: Left at the schema default 0.4 for every entry. No source publishes a match-score threshold, so any other value would be invented.

tagVocabulary.note: Consumed by the rule-based symptom engine (docs/ai/fallback-strategy.md), weights pattern 3, part 2, color 2, distribution 1, weather 1.

diseases.publishedSymptoms: TNAU: "The fungus attacks the crop at all stages of crop growth from seedling to late tillering and ear heading stage." On leaves, "small bluish green flecks" enlarge to form "spindle shaped spots with grey centre and dark brown margin (Leaf blast)". "Black lesions appear on nodes girdling them. The affected nodes may break up and all the plant parts above the infected nodes may die (nodal blast)." "Lesions on the neck are grayish brown and causes the girdling of the neck and the panicle to fall over". "Lesions on the branches of the panicles and on the spikelet pedicels are brown to dark brown". TNAU expert system adds: "white to gray-green lesions or spots with brown borders", "spindle shaped spots(0.5 to 1.5cm length, 0.3 to 0.5cm width) with ashy center", "entire crop give a blasted or burnt appearance", "Nodes become black and break up". Favourable conditions (TNAU expert system): "cloudy skies, frequent rain, and drizzles", "high relative humidity (90% and higher) and wet leaves", "temperature from 25-28°C", "high nitrogen levels like ammonium sulfate".
diseases.tagDerivation: part:LEAF from "spindle shaped spots ... (Leaf blast)"; part:STEM from "Black lesions appear on nodes girdling them" (the node is on the culm); pattern:SPOTS from "spindle shaped spots"; pattern:LESIONS from "Black lesions appear on nodes"; color:GREY from "grey centre" / "ashy center"; color:BROWN from "dark brown margin"; color:BLACK from "Nodes become black"; weather:HIGH_HUMIDITY from "high relative humidity (90% and higher) and wet leaves"; weather:RAIN from "frequent rain, and drizzles". No distribution tag: neither page states whether lower or upper leaves are affected first.

names.en: Brown spot of rice (sesame leaf spot)

diseases.publishedSymptoms: TNAU: "minute spots on the coleoptile, leaf blade, leaf sheath, and glume"; the spots are "cylindrical or oval, dark brown with yellow halo"; "the leaf dries up"; "seedlings die and affected nurseries can be often recognised from a distance by scorched appearance"; "Dark brown or black spots also appear on glumes leading to grain discoloration"; the disease causes "failure of seed germination, seedling mortality and reduces the grain quality and weight". TNAU expert system adds: "The disease appears first as minute brown dots, later becoming cylindrical or oval to circular"; "Spots measures 0.5 to 2.0mm in breadth - coalesce to form large patches"; "Infection also occurs on panicle, neck with brown colour appearance"; "Seeds also infected (black or brown spots on glumes)". Favourable conditions: "Temperature of 25-30°C", "Relative humidity above 80 per cent", "Excess of nitrogen aggravates the disease incidence", "Leaves must be wet for 8-24 hours for infection to occur".
diseases.tagDerivation: part:LEAF from "minute spots on the coleoptile, leaf blade, leaf sheath"; pattern:SPOTS from "cylindrical or oval" spots; color:BROWN from "dark brown with yellow halo"; color:YELLOW from "yellow halo"; color:BLACK from "Dark brown or black spots also appear on glumes"; weather:HIGH_HUMIDITY from "Relative humidity above 80 per cent" and "Leaves must be wet for 8-24 hours". No distribution tag is published. Glume/panicle infection is published but the vocabulary has no part tag for grain, glume or panicle (gap D7).

diseases.publishedSymptoms: TNAU: the disease shows as "Leaf blight, kresek (the seedling blight or wilt phase) and the pale-yellow leaf"; "Seedlings in the nursery show circular, yellow spots in the margin, that enlarge, coalesce"; "Water soaked, translucent lesions appear near the leaf margin"; "Lesions enlarge both in length and width with a wavy margin and turn straw yellow"; "Milky or opaque dew drops containing bacterial masses are formed on young lesions". TNAU expert system adds, for the kresek phase, symptoms "Observed 1-3 weeks after transplanting" with a "green water-soaked layer along the cut portion or leaf tip of leaves", the seedlings wilting and rolling and turning "grayish green to yellow"; and for leaf blight "Water-soaked to yellowish stripes on leaf blades or starting at leaf tips with a wavy margin", "undulated yellowish white or golden yellow marginal necrosis, drying of leaves back from tip and curling, leaving mid rib intact", and "bacterial ooze that looks like a milky or opaque dewdrop on young lesions" seen in the early morning. Favourable conditions: "Clipping of tip of the seedling at the time of transplanting", "Heavy rain, heavy dew, flooding, deep irrigation water", "Severe wind and temperature of 25-30°C", "Application of excessive nitrogen, especially late top dressing", and "presence of weeds".
diseases.tagDerivation: part:LEAF from "lesions appear near the leaf margin"; pattern:LESIONS from "Water soaked, translucent lesions"; pattern:STREAKS from "Water-soaked to yellowish stripes on leaf blades"; pattern:YELLOWING from "turn straw yellow" and "golden yellow marginal necrosis"; pattern:CURL from "drying of leaves back from tip and curling"; color:YELLOW from "straw yellow" / "yellowish white or golden yellow"; distribution:MARGINS from "near the leaf margin" and "marginal necrosis"; weather:HIGH_HUMIDITY from "high humidity" and "heavy dew"; weather:RAIN from "Heavy rain". No color tag for "straw" or "milky/opaque" — the closest, color:TAN, is not the published word and was not used.

diseases.publishedSymptoms: TNAU: "Plants affected by tungro exhibit stunting and reduced tillering"; "Leaves become yellow or orange-yellow, it may also have rust-colored spots"; "Yellowing starts from the tip of the leaf and may extend to the lower part"; "Young leaves are often mottled with pale green to whitish interveinal stripes"; "Delayed flowering - panicles are small and not completely exerted"; "Most panicles are sterile or partially filled grains". Causal agents: "Rice tungro bacilliform virus (RTBV) and Rice tungro spherical virus (RTSV)". Vector: "Green leafhopper, Nephotettix virescens". Factors favouring development: "Presence of the virus sources", "Presence of the vector", "Age and susceptibility of host plants", "Synchronization of the three above factors", "All growth stages of rice plant specifically the vegetative stage".
diseases.tagDerivation: part:LEAF from "Leaves become yellow or orange-yellow"; part:WHOLE_PLANT from "Plants affected by tungro exhibit stunting and reduced tillering"; pattern:YELLOWING from "Yellowing starts from the tip of the leaf"; pattern:STUNTING from "stunting and reduced tillering"; pattern:STREAKS from "whitish interveinal stripes"; pattern:MOSAIC from "Young leaves are often mottled" (mottling is the published word for the mosaic pattern); pattern:SPOTS from "rust-colored spots"; color:YELLOW and color:ORANGE from "yellow or orange-yellow"; color:WHITE from "pale green to whitish"; distribution:VEINS from "interveinal stripes". No weather tag: the published favourable-conditions list is entirely about virus source, vector and host age, not weather.

diseases.publishedSymptoms: TNAU field diagnostic symptoms: "Brown spots with concentric rings in a bull's eye pattern with yellow margin"; "Fruit gets infected through calyx or stem attachment"; "Brown concentric rings on fruits". Favourable conditions: "Warm, humid (24-29 degree C), rainy and wet weather". NIPHM adds: "Early blight is first observed on the plants as small, black lesions mostly on the older foliage"; "Spots enlarge, and by the time they are one-fourth inch in diameter or larger, concentric rings in a bull's eye pattern can be seen in the center of the diseased area"; "Tissue surrounding the spots may turn yellow. If high temperature and humidity occur at this time, much of the foliage is killed"; "Lesions on the stems are similar to those on leaves, sometimes girdling the plant if they occur near the soil line"; "Lesions attain considerable size, usually involving nearly the entire fruit; concentric rings are also present on the fruit". NIPHM favourable conditions: "Warm, rainy and wet weather". NIPHM survival: "The fungus spends the winter in infected plant debris in or on the soil where it can survive at least one and perhaps several years. It can also be seed borne."
diseases.tagDerivation: part:LEAF from "small, black lesions mostly on the older foliage"; part:STEM from "Lesions on the stems are similar to those on leaves"; part:FRUIT from "Brown concentric rings on fruits"; pattern:SPOTS from "Brown spots"; pattern:RINGS from "concentric rings in a bull's eye pattern"; color:BROWN from "Brown spots"; color:BLACK from "small, black lesions"; color:YELLOW from "with yellow margin" and "Tissue surrounding the spots may turn yellow"; distribution:LOWER_LEAVES from "mostly on the older foliage"; weather:HIGH_HUMIDITY from "Warm, humid (24-29 degree C)"; weather:RAIN from "rainy and wet weather".

Favourable conditions: "moist weather and splattering rains"; "high humidity or persistent dew". diseases.classCodeCaveat: The ML class code is TOMATO_YELLOW_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS (PlantVillage nomenclature, i.e. Tomato yellow leaf curl virus, TYLCV). The Indian sources fetched publish the disease as 'Tomato leaf curl virus (ToLCV)' — an Indian begomovirus complex, whitefly-transmitted like TYLCV but not the same virus. names.en therefore uses the published Indian name, not the ML class label. See gap D2.
diseases.publishedSymptoms: TNAU field diagnostic symptoms: "Severe stunting of plants"; "Downward rolling and crinkling of the leaves"; "Older leaves become leathery and brittle"; "Shortening of internodes"; "Appearence of more lateral branches - bushy appearance". NIPHM adds: "The newly emerging leaves exhibit slight yellow colouration and later they also show curling symptoms"; "The infected plants look pale and produce more lateral branches giving a bushy appearance. The infected plants remain stunted." NIPHM favourable conditions: "whitefly is the vector for transmitting of leaf curl virus".

On fruit, damage begins as "small, brown, sunken flecks" that expand into deeply pitted lesions, often producing an X- or star-shaped cracking pattern on severely affected fruit. gaps.field: TOMATO_YELLOW_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS — the class code does not match the disease the Indian sources describe
gaps.problem: The ML class code follows PlantVillage and names Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV). Every Indian source fetched publishes the Indian disease as 'Tomato leaf curl virus (ToLCV)' — a distinct begomovirus complex. Both are transmitted by Bemisia tabaci and their field symptoms overlap heavily, but they are not the same virus, and the Indian sources' symptom emphasis is DOWNWARD rolling while TYLCV literature emphasises UPWARD curling.
gaps.checked: TNAU tomato_diseases_6.html ('Leaf curl: Tomato leaf curl virus'); NIPHM Tomato IPM roster item 2.2 ('Tomato leaf curl virus (ToLCV)') and description 7) Leaf curl. Searched for an Indian official page naming TYLCV specifically — none found; the TYLCV-specific results were all US/EU extension or journal literature.
gaps.impact: A model trained on the PlantVillage TYLCV class will be labelled, in the app, with an Indian disease name and Indian symptom text. That is arguably the RIGHT product decision for Indian farmers, but it is a substitution and must be a conscious one.
gaps.resolution: names.en records the published Indian name; `classCodeCaveat` on the entry states the substitution explicitly. Needs a human decision before ship. Do NOT quietly rename the ML class.

gaps.problem: The NIPHM tomato package prints 'Favourable conditions: Warm weather conditions are favourable for multiplication' immediately BEFORE the spider-mite section heading, i.e. it belongs to the preceding pest, not to mites. Hot dry weather is the classic driver of mite outbreaks, which would help discriminate mites from the fungal leaf spots, but it is not published in any source fetched here.

gaps.field: symptomTags vocabulary — concepts published by the sources that have no tag
gaps.problem: Five published, diagnostically important concepts have no member in the closed vocabulary: (a) MOULD or VELVETY FUNGAL GROWTH on a leaf surface — the single most diagnostic feature of tomato leaf mould, and also how potato/tomato late blight sporulation is described ('white growth', 'looks like flour'); pattern:POWDER was NOT reused for it, because POWDER denotes powdery mildew and reusing it would make leaf mould collide with the powdery-mildew classes another part of this KB will carry. (b) LEAF UNDERSIDE as a distribution — sources repeatedly say 'under surface of leaves', which the vocabulary cannot express. (c) GREEN as a colour — 'light and dark green mottling' (tomato mosaic) and 'bluish green flecks' (rice blast) cannot be coloured at all. (d) A part tag for GRAIN / PANICLE / GLUME — rice brown spot and blast both describe glume and panicle infection. (e) A part tag for TUBER.

gaps.impact: TOMATO_LEAF_MOLD in particular loses its strongest discriminator and is left matching on generic 'yellow-brown spots on lower leaves', which collides with early blight and Septoria. TOMATO_MOSAIC_VIRUS carries no colour tag at all, forfeiting the colour term (weight 2). Rice glume/panicle symptoms and potato tuber symptoms are unreachable by the questionnaire.

Tuber symptoms were mapped to part:ROOT for POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT as the only available underground-part tag, and that mapping is labelled a decision rather than a source claim in that entry's tagDerivation. Recommend the vocabulary gain pattern:MOULD, distribution:LEAF_UNDERSIDE, color:GREEN, part:GRAIN and part:TUBER before this KB is relied on for the no-photo path.

gaps.problem: The stage-wise practice table in the tomato package extracts from PDF with rows and columns interleaved: a 'Cultural control' bullet list can appear several lines away from the disease name it belongs to, and adjacent rows' text is spliced. Two practice blocks used here were attributed by reading the surrounding page structure rather than by an unambiguous heading.
gaps.checked: Manual reading of the pdftotext -layout output around each block, cross-checked against the disease name printed nearest above it. The 'Field sanitation / Destruction of alternate hosts / Provide light irrigation' block sits under the row headed 'Alternaria blight and late blight'. The 'Conserve predators such as predatory mites (Phytoseiulus spp., Amblyseius spp.)...' block sits in the spider-mite row and its predator list is mite-specific, which corroborates the attribution.
gaps.impact: If either attribution is wrong, a cultural practice is shown against the wrong disease. Both are low-harm, non-chemical, generally-good practices, but that is luck rather than design.
gaps.resolution: Each affected citation names the row heading the block appeared under. A reviewer with the rendered PDF should confirm both. No practice whose row heading could not be read at all was used.

gaps.field: TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT — TNAU prints 'Sporangia formed when RH is < 90%'
gaps.problem: The TNAU tomato late-blight page lists as a favourable condition 'Sporangia formed when RH is < 90%'. Every other statement on the same page (and the potato late-blight page's 'RH->90%') points the other way; this reads as an inverted inequality.
gaps.checked: https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/crop_protection/tomato_diseases_8.html against https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/crop_protection/crop_prot_crop%20diseases_veg_potato_1.html and the NIPHM potato package's 'High humidity'.
gaps.impact: If surfaced, a farmer could be told sporulation needs LOW humidity, which would invert the weather advice for the fastest-moving disease in this file.
gaps.resolution: The line is recorded in publishedSymptoms and in the citation note for the record, but is NOT rendered into any farmer-facing i18n string, and weather:HIGH_HUMIDITY was NOT tagged from it (the tags come from 'Cool nights, warm days and extended wet conditions' instead). Needs TNAU verification.

gaps.problem: The NIPHM tomato package lists late blight in its disease roster (2.4) but its 'VIII. Description of diseases' section jumps from bacterial leaf spot to bacterial wilt with no late-blight entry. The symptom description therefore rests on the TNAU page alone, with no Indian second source.
gaps.checked: Full enumeration of the description section in the pdftotext output: damping off, Septoria leaf spot, bacterial stem and fruit canker, early blight, bacterial leaf spot, bacterial wilt, leaf curl, mosaic, spotted wilt, Fusarium wilt. No late blight.
gaps.impact: Single-source symptomology for one of the two highest-consequence tomato diseases in the roster.
gaps.resolution: Recorded. The NIPHM potato late-blight description WAS available and is cited on POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT; the same pathogen's tomato description should be sourced from a second Indian page before ship.

gaps.field: POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT — TNAU prints 'Shot holes on fruits'
gaps.problem: The TNAU potato early-blight page lists 'Shot holes on fruits' among the symptoms. Potato is a tuber crop; farmers do not inspect potato fruit. The line appears to be carried over from a solanaceous fruit-crop page.
gaps.checked: https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/crop_protection/crop_prot_crop%20diseases_veg_potato_2.html; compared against the NIPHM potato early-blight description, which describes leaf, stem and tuber only and never mentions fruit or shot holes.
gaps.impact: Tagging part:FRUIT and pattern:HOLES from this line would have made POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT match a farmer answering 'holes in fruit' — a wrong answer produced by a source typo.
gaps.resolution: The line is preserved verbatim in publishedSymptoms but is NOT tagged and NOT rendered into any farmer-facing string.

gaps.field: nextSteps — every disease whose source recommends chemical control
gaps.problem: Every TNAU and NIPHM page used here publishes fungicide, bactericide, acaricide or insecticide recommendations, most with product names and rates (e.g. rice blast, rice brown spot, rice BLB, rice tungro, tomato early/late blight, tomato leaf curl, tomato spider mites, potato early/late blight).
gaps.checked: Each cited page was read in full; the chemical blocks are noted in each sourceRef's `note` so a reviewer can see that they exist and were deliberately dropped.
gaps.impact: The KB gives a farmer facing an active epidemic no chemical option, which for potato late blight ('infected plants will die within two or three days') is a real limitation of the product, not a data gap.
gaps.resolution: docs/ai/ai-safety.md rule 3 is absolute: no dosage generation anywhere. Each affected entry carries a nextStep key routing the farmer to KVK / Kisan Call Centre 1800-180-1551. No product name, active ingredient, concentration or rate appears anywhere in this file or its companion. The one number reproduced from a management block is a yellow-sticky-trap density (traps per acre), which is a device count, not a dose.

gaps.field: Healthy classes — 'what healthy looks like' is not published anywhere
gaps.problem: No source fetched describes a healthy rice, tomato or potato plant. Extension material describes disease, never health. Writing 'a healthy plant has uniformly green leaves with no spots' would have been an invented description built by negating the disease entries.
gaps.checked: TNAU crop-protection pages (disease-only by construction); all three NIPHM AESA packages — the closest published material is the AESA/scouting methodology and the 'Grow a healthy crop' principle list, both of which describe what the FARMER should DO, not what a healthy plant LOOKS like.
gaps.impact: The healthy classes cannot tell a farmer 'this is what a healthy leaf looks like'. They can only tell them how to inspect and what to keep doing.
gaps.resolution: inspect keys for the three healthy classes carry the published observation methodology (weekly monitoring, five random spots and five plants per spot for tomato, leaf undersides, morning AESA before 9 a.m. for rice, ETL thresholds for rice) and prevention carries the published 'Grow a healthy crop' practices. Nothing about leaf appearance is asserted. If a visual healthy-plant description is wanted, it must be authored by an agronomist and marked as such.

gaps.problem: No source publishes anything resembling a symptom-match confidence threshold; 0.4 is the CropRegistry schema default and matches the 'score <0.4 → contact KVK/Kisan Call Centre' rule already written into docs/ai/fallback-strategy.md.
gaps.impact: None yet. But diseases with weak tag sets (TOMATO_LEAF_MOLD, TOMATO_MOSAIC_VIRUS — see D7) will systematically score lower, so a uniform threshold routes them to a human more often than better-tagged diseases. That is the safe direction of failure, and is noted rather than tuned.
gaps.resolution: Left at the default for every entry. Any per-disease value would be an invented number.

gaps.problem: The host is intermittently unreliable. Two fetches failed with 'certificate has expired' and succeeded on retry minutes later (rice_1.html, cpdisblast.html, tomato_diseases_10.html). The www. variant fails outright: 'Hostname/IP does not match certificate's altnames: Host: www.agritech.tnau.ac.in is not in the cert's altnames: DNS:agritech.tnau.ac.in'. Separately, cpri.icar.gov.in did not resolve at all ('getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND'), so the ICAR-CPRI potato disease manual could not be fetched and TNAU + NIPHM were used for potato instead.
gaps.checked: Every fetch in this pass. Also note the TNAU tomato index numbering is unreliable: the index lists tomato_diseases_9.html as 'Leaf Curl', but that URL serves bacterial stem and fruit canker; the real leaf-curl page is tomato_diseases_6.html, which the index labels 'Bacterial Canker'.
gaps.impact: Any automated re-verification of these citations will see intermittent failures that are not evidence the content changed. The index/URL mismatch means a future researcher following the index alone would cite the wrong page for leaf curl.
gaps.resolution: Recorded, mirroring gap L8 in crops.limited.proposal.json. Every URL in this file was fetched and its CONTENT verified against the disease it is cited for — the index labels were not trusted. Retry on 'certificate has expired'; never use the www. prefix. ICAR-CPRI should be retried for potato when DNS resolves.
